<!-- ex-1: body_md -->
\label{eg single point hom} Consider an empty hypergraph $G$. Then 
$
Q_n^*(G)=D_n^*(G)=C_n^*(G)=\{0\} \quad \text{for all } n \geq 0.
$
If $G$ consists of a single vertex with a hyperedge containing it, then there is exactly one nondegenerate $(0,*)$-hypercube. Thus,
$
C_0^*(G)=Q_0^*(G)\cong \mathbb{Z},
$
while for all $n>0$, every $(n,*)$-hypercube is degenerate, so $C_n^*(G)=\{0\}$. Hence,
\[
H_n^*(G)=
\begin{cases}
\mathbb{Z} & n=0,\\
\{0\} & n \geq 1.
\end{cases}
\]
The same conclusion holds if $G$ has $n$ vertices with a single hyperedge containing all of them.
\\
Also, if $G$ consists of a single vertex with no hyperedge, then 
\[
C_n^*(G)=\{0\} \quad \text{for all } n \geq 0,
\]
and hence 
\[
H_n^*(G)=\{0\} \quad \text{for all } n \geq 0.
\]
<!-- end ex-1 -->
<!-- prop-1: body_md -->
\label{prop 1-connected}
	If a hypergraph $G$ is $1$-connected, then $H_0^*(G)\cong \mathbb{Z}$.
<!-- end prop-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Define $\epsilon:C_0^*(G)\to \mathbb{Z}$ by
\[
\epsilon\Big(\sum_i n_i \sigma_i\Big)=\sum_i n_i.
\]
Since $C_0^*(G)=Z_0^*(G)$, it suffices to show $\ker(\epsilon)=B_0^*(G)$.

For $\sum_i n_i \sigma_i \in C_1^*(G)$,
\[
\partial_1\Big(\sum_i n_i \sigma_i\Big)
= \sum_i n_i (B_1\sigma_i - A_1\sigma_i),
\]
so $\epsilon\circ \partial_1=0$, and hence $B_0^*(G)\subseteq \ker(\epsilon)$.

Conversely, let $\sum_i n_i v_i \in \ker(\epsilon)$, so $\sum_i n_i=0$. Fix $v\in V$. For each $v_i$, $1$-connectedness gives a sequence of hyperedges joining $v$ to $v_i$ through a sequence $v=v_{i_0},v_{i_1},\ldots,v_{i_k}=v_i$ such that for $j=1,\ldots,k-1$, each $v_{i_j}$ contained in the intersection of the hyperedges, yielding $(1,*)$-hypercubes of the form \[\sigma_{i_j}:J_1^*\to G\] with $\sigma_{i_j}(0)=v_{i_{j-1}}$ and $\sigma_{i_j}(1)=v_{i_j}$ such that 
\[
\partial_1\Big(\sum_j^k\sigma_{i_j}\Big)=v_{i_k} - v_{i_0}=v_i-v.
\]
Thus,
\[
\partial_1\Big(\sum_{i,j} n_i \sigma_{i_j}\Big)
= \sum_i n_i v_i - \Big(\sum_i n_i\Big)v
= \sum_i n_i v_i,
\]
so $\ker(\epsilon)\subseteq B_0^*(G)$.

Therefore, $\ker(\epsilon)=B_0^*(G)$ and
\[
H_0^*(G)=Z_0^*(G)/B_0^*(G)\cong \mathbb{Z}.
\]
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- prop-2: body_md -->
Let hypergragh $G=(V,E)$ and $G_1$ and $G_2$ be the non empty subhypergaphs such that $V=V_1 \bigsqcup V_2$ and $E= E(V_1) \bigsqcup E(V_2)$, where $V_1$ and $V_2$ are vertex sets of $G_1$ and $G_2$, respectively. Then $H_n^*(G)=H_n^*(G_1)\oplus H_n^*(G_2)$.
<!-- end prop-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
We will just sketch the proof. For the case of $H_n^*(G)$ note that by definition of hypergraph morphism, $C_n^*(G)=C_n^*(G_1)\oplus C_n^*(G_2)$ and the result follows.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- ex-2: body_md -->
\label{eg gamma 3-cycle}
Let $G=(V,E)$ be the hypergraph with vertex set $V=\{a,b,c\}$ and hyperedge set $E=\{\{a,b\},\{a,c\},\{b,c\}\}$. Then
\[
C_0^\Gamma(G)=\langle a,b,c \rangle \cong \mathbb{Z}^3,
\]
and
\[
C_1^\Gamma(G)=\langle \sigma_{ab}, \sigma_{ba}, \sigma_{ac}, \sigma_{ca}, \sigma_{bc}, \sigma_{cb} \rangle,
\]
where $\sigma_{ab}(0)=a$ and $\sigma_{ab}(1)=b$.
\\
A direct computation (via the Smith normal form of $\partial_1$) shows that
\[
Z_1^\Gamma(G)\cong \mathbb{Z}^4, \quad B_0^\Gamma(G)\cong \mathbb{Z}^2,
\]
and hence $H_0^\Gamma(G)\cong \mathbb{Z}$.
\\
Similarly, boundaries of the $(2,\Gamma)$-cubes $\sigma_{abaa}, \sigma_{acaa}, \sigma_{bcbb}$ generate $\operatorname{Im}(\partial_2)\cong \mathbb{Z}^3$, yielding
\[
H_1^\Gamma(G)\cong \mathbb{Z}.
\]
<!-- end ex-2 -->
<!-- ex-3: body_md -->
\label{eg x and box hom} 
	Let $G=(V,E)$ be the hypergraph with vertex set $V=\{a,b,c\}$ and set of hyperedges $E=\{\{a,b\},\{b,c\},\{a,c\}\}$. We have \[{C}_0^\times(G)=\langle \sigma_a,\sigma_b,\sigma_c\rangle \cong \mathbb{Z}^3\] where $\sigma_a,\sigma_b,$ and $\sigma_c$ are  $(0,\times)$-hypercubes. 	
    \[{C}_1^\times(G)=\langle \sigma_{ab},\sigma_{ba},\sigma_{bc},\sigma_{cb},\sigma_{ca},\sigma_{ac}\rangle \cong \mathbb{Z}^6.\] Then after computing boundary matrix of $\partial_1$ we have  \[{Z}_1^\times(G)\cong\mathbb{Z}^4 ~\text{and} ~ {B}_0^\times(G)=\mathbb{Z}^2.\] Hence, \[H_0^\times(G)=\mathbb{Z}.\] There are 48 non-degenerate $(2,\times)$-hypercubes, and after computation we have, \[{B}_1(J_1^\times,G)\cong \mathbb{Z}^4, \] and thus, \[H_1^\times(G)\cong \{0\}.\] Similar computation with same hypergraph $G$ gives \[H_1^\Box(G)\cong \{0\}.\]
<!-- end ex-3 -->
<!-- ex-4: body_md -->
\label{eg box and x 1-hom}
Let $G=(V,E)$ with $V=\{a,b,c,d\}$ and $E=\{\{a,b\}, \{a,d\},\\ \{b,c\}, \{c,d\}\}$ then \[{C}_0^\Box(G)={Z}_0^\Box(G)=\mathbb{Z}^4\] and \[{C}_1^\Box(G)=\langle \sigma_{ab}, \sigma_{ba},\sigma_{ad},\sigma_{da},\sigma_{bc},\sigma_{cb}, \sigma_{cd},\sigma_{dc}\rangle.\] After the computation of the boundary matrix $\partial_{1}({C}_1^\Box(G))$, we have \[{Z}_1^\Box(G)=\mathbb{Z}^5 \text{ and } {B}_0^\Box(G)=\mathbb{Z}^3.\] Thus, \[H_0^\Box(G)= \mathbb{Z}.\] The Rank of the boundary matrix $\partial_{2}({C}_2^\Box(G))$ is $5$. Hence, \[H_1^\Box(G)=\{0\}.\] Note that, \[{C}_0^\times(G)={Z}_0^\times(G)=\mathbb{Z}^4.\] Now, the computation of the boundary matrix of $\partial_1({C}_1^\times(G))$ gives, \[{Z}_1^\times(G)=\mathbb{Z}^5 \text{ and } {B}_0^\times(G)=\mathbb{Z}^3.\] Thus, \[H_0^\times(G)=\mathbb{Z}.\] Rank of the boundary matrix of $\partial_{2}({C}_2^\times(G))$ is 4. Hence \[H_1^\times(G)=\mathbb{Z}.\]
<!-- end ex-4 -->
<!-- def-1: body_md -->
\label{def_Gmn}
For integers $m\ge2$ and $n\ge1$, define the $m$-uniform hypergraph $G_n^m$ recursively as follows. Let $G_1^m$ consist of three hyperedges
\[
e_1,e_2,e_3
\]
such that
\[
|e_1\cap e_2|
=
|e_2\cap e_3|
=
|e_3\cap e_1|
=1,
\]
with the three pairwise intersections distinct. For $n\ge2$, obtain $G_n^m$ from $G_{n-1}^m$ by choosing an end hyperedge $e_{2n-1}$ and adjoining two new $m$-element hyperedges $e_{2n}$ and $e_{2n+1}$ such that
\[
|e_{2n-1}\cap e_{2n}|
=
|e_{2n}\cap e_{2n+1}|
=
|e_{2n+1}\cap e_{2n-1}|
=1,
\]
where these three intersection vertices are distinct, and such that
$e_{2n}$ and $e_{2n+1}$ have no other vertices in common with $G_{n-1}^m$.
<!-- end def-1 -->
<!-- prop-3: body_md -->
\label{prop_h1_Gmn}
Let $m=2$ and $n\ge1$. Then
\[
H_1^\Gamma(G_n^2)\cong \mathbb{Z}^n.
\]
<!-- end prop-3 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
We first note that the hypergraph $G_n^2$ has    $2n+1$ hyperedges, it has $n+2$ vertices. Since $G_{n}^2$ has $n+2$ vertices, 
    \[C_0^\Gamma(G_{n}^2)=Z_0^\Gamma(G_{n}^2)\cong \mathbb{Z}^{n+2}. \] 
    Since $G_{n}^2$  is a 1-connected hypergraph we have $H_0^\Gamma(G_{n}^2)\cong\mathbb{Z}$, 
    therefore
            \[ B_0^\Gamma(G_{n}^2)\cong \mathbb{Z}^{n+1}.
           \]
           Furthermore, $G_{n}^2$ has $2n+1$  hyperedges. 
           Since each
hyperedge with vertices $a,b$ gives rise to two generators
$\sigma_{ab}$ and $\sigma_{ba}$ of $C_1^\Gamma(G_{n+1}^2)$, we have,
           \[ C_1^\Gamma(G_{n}^2)\cong \mathbb{Z}^{4n+2}, \] which implies \[Z_1^\Gamma(G_{n}^2)\cong \mathbb{Z}^{3n+1}.\] 
           For each hyperedge with vertices $a,b$, boundary of the singular $(2,\Gamma)$-hypercube $\sigma_{abaa}$ equals $\sigma_{ab}+\sigma_{ba}$. 
           Therefore, two generators of 
           $C_1^\Gamma(G_{n}^2)$
           contribute to one generator
           \[
           \sigma_{ab}+\sigma_{ba}\in B_1^
           \Gamma(G_{n}^2)\]
           Since the hyperedges are distinct, these
relations are independent,
           therefore the rank of
           $B_1^\Gamma(G_{n}^2)$ equals half the rank of $C_1^\Gamma(G_{n}^2)$. 
           We have \[  B_1^\Gamma(G_{n}^2)\cong \mathbb{Z}^{2n+1}.\]  
           Hence, \[H_1^\Gamma(G_{n}^2)=\frac{\mathbb{Z}^{3n+1}}{\mathbb{Z}^{2n+1}}\cong \mathbb{Z}^{n}.\]
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- ex-5: body_md -->
\label{general 3-cycle}
Let $G$ be the hypergraph with
\[
V=\{a,b,c,d,e\}, \quad E=\{\{a,b,c\},\{b,e\},\{c,d\},\{d,e\}\}.
\]
A direct computation shows
\[
H_1^\Gamma(G)\cong \mathbb{Z}.
\]
<!-- end ex-5 -->
<!-- rem-1: body_md -->
The above example \ref{general 3-cycle} shows that $\Gamma$-homology captures not only uniform cycles but also non-uniform cycle structures. Furthermore,  examples \ref{eg gamma 3-cycle} and \ref{eg box and x 1-hom} show that the $\Gamma$-homology and the $\times$-homology, respectively, for graphs (2-uniform hypergraphs), detects $3$-cycles and $4$-cycles, unlike discrete cubical homology.
<!-- end rem-1 -->
<!-- def-2: body_md -->
Let $G=(V,E)$ and $G'=(V',E')$ be hypergraphs, and let $f,g:G\rightarrow G'$ be hypergraph morphisms. We say that $f$ is \emph{$m$-step homotopic} to $g$, denoted by $f\simeq_m g$, if there exists a hypergraph morphism
\[
F:G\times J_m \rightarrow G'
\]
such that
\begin{itemize}
	\item $F(v,0)=f(v)$ for all $v\in V$,
	\item $F(v,m)=g(v)$ for all $v\in V$,
\end{itemize}
where $J_m$ is the hypergraph with vertex set $\{0,1,\ldots,m\}$ and hyperedges $\{\{0,1\},\ldots,\{m-1,m\}\}$.
<!-- end def-2 -->
<!-- def-3: body_md -->
Two hypergraphs $G$ and $H$ are said to be \emph{homotopy equivalent} if there exist hypergraph morphisms $f:G\rightarrow H$ and $g:H\rightarrow G$ such that
\[
f\circ g \simeq Id_H \quad \text{and} \quad g\circ f \simeq Id_G.
\]
<!-- end def-3 -->
<!-- con-1: body_md -->
\label{dual HE}
	Let $G$ be a hypergraph and $G^*$ its dual. Then $G\simeq G^*$.
<!-- end con-1 -->
<!-- thm-1: body_md -->
\label{thm 2}
Let $f,g:G\rightarrow H$ be hypergraph morphisms. If $f\simeq_m g$, then
\[
f_*= g_*:H_n^\Box(G)\rightarrow H_n^\Box(H).
\]
<!-- end thm-1 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
Define $F_j(x,t)=F(x,j+t-1)$, where $j\in [1,m]_{\mathbb{Z}}$, using the homotopy $F$. Construct chain homotopies $\phi_n$ by
	\[
	\phi_n(\sigma)(x_1,\ldots,x_{n+1})=F_j(\sigma(x_1,\ldots,x_n),x_{n+1}).
	\]
	A direct computation shows
	\[
	g_{\#}-f_{\#}=\partial_{n+1}\phi_n+\phi_{n-1}\partial_n.
	\]
	Hence $f_*=g_*$.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- prop-4: body_md -->
\label{homotopy equivalent}
	If $G\simeq H$, then
	\[
	H_n^\Box(G)\cong H_n^\Box(H).
	\]
<!-- end prop-4 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
Follows immediately from Theorem \ref{thm 2}.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- ex-6: body_md -->
Let $G=(V,E)$ and $H=(V',E')$ be hypergraphs with
\[
V=\{a,b,c,d\}, \quad V'=\{u,w,x,y,z\},
\]
\[
E=\{\{a,b,c\},\{a,c\},\{c\},\{a,c,d\}\}, \quad
E'=\{\{x,y,z\},\{u,x,y\},\{u,x,w\}\}.
\]
Define morphisms $f,g:G\to H$ by
\[
f(a)=w,\; f(b)=x,\; f(c)=u,\; f(d)=x,
\]
\[
g(a)=y,\; g(b)=z,\; g(c)=x,\; g(d)=u.
\]
Then $f\simeq_5 g$ via the homotopy given in the following table.
	{\fontsize{8.5pt}{10pt}\selectfont
    \[ \begin{tabular}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|}
		\hline
		$F(X,0)$& $F(X,1)$ & $F(X,2)$ & $F(X,3)$ & $F(X,4)$ & $F(X,5)$ \\
		\hline
		$F(a,0)=f(a)=w$&  $F(a,1)=x$ & $F(a,2)=y$& $F(a,3)= y$  & $F(a,4)= y$ &  $F(a,5)= y=g(a)$\\
		\hline
		$F(b,0)=f(b)=x$&  $F(b,1)=x$ & $F(b,2)=x$ & $F(b,3)=x$ & $F(b,4)=x $  & $F(b,5)= z=g(b)$ \\
		\hline
		$F(c,0)=f(c)=u$ & $F(c,1)=u$ & $F(c,2)=u$ & $F(c,3)=x$ & $F(c,4)= x$ & $F(c,5)=x=g(c)$ \\
		\hline
		$F(d,0)=f(d)=x$& $F(d,1)=x$ & $F(d,2)=x$ & $F(d,3)$=x & $F(d,4)=u$ & $F(d,5)=u=g(d)$ \\
		\hline
	\end{tabular}
	\]}
<!-- end ex-6 -->
<!-- ex-7: body_md -->
\label{eg not homotopy invariant}
Let $G$ be the hypergraph with vertex set $V=\{a,b,c,d\}$ and hyperedge set $E=\{\{a,b\},\{b,c\},\{c,d\},\{a,d\}\}$, and let $G'$ be the hypergraph with $V'=\{e\}$ and $E'=\{\{e\}\}$. Define morphisms $f:G\to G'$ by $f(V)=e$ and $g:G'\to G$ by $g(e)=a$ such that $G\simeq G'$. By Example~\ref{eg box and x 1-hom}, \[H_1^\times(G)\cong \mathbb{Z} \text{ and } H_1^\Gamma(G)\cong \mathbb{Z},\] whereas by example~\ref{eg single point hom} we have,
\[H_1^\times(G')=\{0\} \text{ and } H_1^\Gamma(G')=\{0\}.\]
<!-- end ex-7 -->
<!-- def-4: body_md -->
\label{def:neighborhood}
Let $G = (V,E)$ be a hypergraph and let $x \in V$. The \emph{neighborhood} of $x$ in $G$ is the induced subhypergraph $N(x,G)$ with vertex set
\[
V(N(x,G)) = \{ y \in V \mid \exists\, e \in E \text{ such that } \{x,y\} \subseteq e \}.
\]
<!-- end def-4 -->
<!-- prop-5: body_md -->
\label{prop:closure-interior}
Let $G=(V,E)$ be a hypergraph and let $A,B$ be subhypergraphs of $G$. Then:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item $A \subseteq \operatorname{cl}(A)$ and $\operatorname{int}(A) \subseteq A$.
    \item $\operatorname{int}(G - A) = G - \operatorname{cl}(A)$ and $G - \operatorname{int}(A) = \operatorname{cl}(G - A)$.
    \item If $A \subseteq B$, then $\operatorname{cl}(A) \subseteq \operatorname{cl}(B)$ and $\operatorname{int}(A) \subseteq \operatorname{int}(B)$.
    \item $G = \operatorname{int}(A) \cup \operatorname{int}(B)$ if and only if $\operatorname{cl}(G - B) \subseteq \operatorname{int}(A)$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end prop-5 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
The first two statements follow directly from the definitions. For the identity
\[
G - \operatorname{int}(A) = \operatorname{cl}(G - A),
\]
note that
\[
\operatorname{int}(A) = G - \operatorname{cl}(G - A),
\]
and hence
\[
G - \operatorname{int}(A) = G - (G - \operatorname{cl}(G - A)) = \operatorname{cl}(G - A).
\]
The remaining statements follow immediately from the definitions.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- lem-1: body_md -->
\label{times hom lem}
Let $G=(V,E)$ be the hypergraph, $G_1$ and $G_2$ be any two subhypergraphs such that there is some positive integer $i$ with  $G=\operatorname{int}(G_1)\cup \operatorname{int}(G_2)$. Then for every $(n,\times)$-hyppercube $\sigma$, $Im(\sigma)\subset G_1$ or $Im(\sigma) \subset G_2.$ In particular, $C_n^\times(G)=C_n^\times( G,\mathbb{U})$, where $\mathbb{U}=\{G_1,G_2\}$.
<!-- end lem-1 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
Note that by definition, $C_n^\times(G,\mathbb{U}) \subset C_n^\times(G)$. For converse we proceed through induction,
For $n=0$, let $\sigma \in  C_0^\times(G)$. Clearly, either $Im(\sigma) \in \operatorname{int}(G_1)$ or $Im(\sigma) \in \operatorname{int}(G_2)$. It implies $C_0^\times(G)\subseteq C_0^\times(G,\mathbb{U})$. Let us consider for $n=k$, we have $C_n^\times(G)\subset C_n^\times(G,\mathbb{U})$.

Induction step: $n=k+1$, Assume without loss of generality that $\sigma(S_0) \in \operatorname{int}(G_1).$ Note that,  $\sigma(S_0 \cup S_1 \cup S_2 \cup\ldots \cup S_{k+1}) \subseteq V_1.$ Since all of the vertices of $S_i's$ are in neighbors of $\sigma(S_0)$ in $J^\times_{k+1}$. Thus, $Im(\sigma)\subset G_1$, as desired.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- thm-2: body_md -->
(Excision for $\times$-homology)\\
Let $G=(V,E)$ be hypergraph. Let $G_1=(V_1,E(V_1))$ and $G_2=(V_2,E(V_2))$ are subhypergraph such that $G_1\subseteq G_2$ and $\operatorname{cl}(G_1)\subseteq \operatorname{int}(G_2)$. Then the inclusion $(G-G_1,G_2-G_1)\rightarrow (G,G_2)$ induces isomorpohisms $H_{n}^{\times}(G-G_1,G_2-G_1)\cong H_{n}^{\times}(G,G_2)$ for all $n$. Equivalently, for interior cover $\{A,B\}$ of hypergraph $G=(V,E)$ the inclusion $(B,A\cap B)\rightarrow (G,A)$ induces isomorphisms $H_{n}^{\times}(B,A\cap B)\cong H_{n}^{\times}(G,A), \forall n$.
<!-- end thm-2 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
The result follows directly from Lemma \ref{times hom lem} by a standard argument analogous to the classical case.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- lem-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:Gamma-localization}
Let $G=(V,E)$ be a hypergraph and let $\mathbb{U}=\{G_1,G_2\}$ be a family of subhypergraphs such that
\[
G = \operatorname{int}(G_1) \cup \operatorname{int}(G_2).
\]
Then for $n \in \{0,1,2,3,4\}$,
\[
C_n^\Gamma(G) = C_n^\Gamma(G,\mathbb{U}).
\]
<!-- end lem-2 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
By definition, $C_n^\Gamma(G,\mathbb{U}) \subseteq C_n^\Gamma(G)$. We prove the reverse inclusion.

Let $\sigma : J_n^\Gamma \to G$ be an $(n,\Gamma)$-hypercube. We show that the image of $\sigma$ is contained entirely in $G_1$ or $G_2$.

For $j \ge 0$, recall that
\[
S_j = \{(v_1,\dots,v_n) \in V(J_n^\Gamma) \mid \textstyle\sum_{i=1}^n v_i = j\}.
\]
Note that $S_0$ consists of a single vertex.

Since $G = \operatorname{int}(G_1) \cup \operatorname{int}(G_2)$, we may assume without loss of generality that
\[
\sigma(S_0) \subseteq V(\operatorname{int}(G_1)).
\]
By Definition~\ref{def:neighborhood}, all vertices in $\sigma(S_1)$ and $\sigma(S_2)$ are neighbors of $\sigma(S_0)$, and hence lie in $V(G_1)$. Therefore,
\[
\sigma(S_0 \cup S_1 \cup S_2) \subseteq V(G_1).
\]

If $n \le 2$, it follows immediately that $\operatorname{Im}(\sigma) \subseteq G_1$.

Now suppose $n \in \{3,4\}$. If
\[
\sigma(S_3 \cup S_4) \subseteq V(G_1),
\]
then $\operatorname{Im}(\sigma) \subseteq G_1$, as required.

Otherwise, there exists $x \in S_3 \cup S_4$ such that $\sigma(x) \notin V(G_1)$. Then $\sigma(x) \in V(G \setminus G_1)$, and by Proposition~\ref{prop:closure-interior},
\[
\sigma(S_2 \cup S_3 \cup S_4) \subseteq V(\operatorname{cl}(G - G_1)).
\]
Since $\operatorname{cl}(G - G_1) \subseteq \operatorname{int}(G_2)$, we obtain
\[
\sigma(S_2 \cup S_3 \cup S_4) \subseteq V(\operatorname{int}(G_2)).
\]
Using the definition of interior again, it follows that
\[
\sigma(S_0 \cup S_1) \subseteq V(G_2).
\]
Hence $\operatorname{Im}(\sigma) \subseteq G_2$.

This proves that every $(n,\Gamma)$-hypercube lies in $C_n^\Gamma(G,\mathbb{U})$, and therefore
\[
C_n^\Gamma(G) \subseteq C_n^\Gamma(G,\mathbb{U}).
\]
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- ex-8: body_md -->
Let $G$ be the hypergraph with vertex set $V=\{v_1,\ldots, v_{6}\}$ and set of hyperedges $E=\{\{v_1,v_2,v_3\}, \{v_2, v_3,v_4\},\{v_3,v_4,v_5\}, \{v_4,v_5,v_6\},\}.$ We take $G_1=\{v_1,\ldots, v_5\}$ and $G_2=\{v_2,\ldots, v_{6}\}$. Note that $\operatorname{int}(G_1)=\{v_1,v_2,v_3\}$ and $\operatorname{int}(G_2)=\{v_4,v_5,v_{6}\}$ and thus $G=\operatorname{int}(G_1)\cup \operatorname{int}(G_2)$. Now define $\sigma: J_5^\Gamma\rightarrow G$ by $\sigma(S_0)=v_1$, $\sigma(S_1)=v_2$, $\sigma(S_2)=v_3$, $\sigma(S_3)=v_4$, $\sigma(S_4)=v_5$ and $\sigma(S_5)=v_{6}$. Note that $\sigma $ is a hypergraph morhism and $Im(\sigma) \notin G_i$ for $i=\{1,2\}$.
<!-- end ex-8 -->
<!-- thm-3: body_md -->
\label{gamma excision}
	(Excision-like for $\Gamma$-homology)\\
	Let $G=(V,E)$ be hypergraph. Let $G_1=(V_1,E_1)$ and $G_2=(V_2,E_2)$ are  subhypergraphs such that $G_1\subseteq G_2$ and $\operatorname{cl}(G_1)\subseteq \operatorname{int}(G_2)$. Then the inclusion $(G-G_1,G_2-G_1)\rightarrow (G,G_2)$ induces isomorpohisms $H_{n}^\Gamma(G-G_1,G_2-G_1)\cong H_{n}^\Gamma(G,G_2)$ for all $n<4$. Equivalently, for interior cover $\{A,B\}$ of hypergraph $G=(V,E)$ the inclusion $(B,A\cap B)\rightarrow (G,A)$ induces isomorphisms $H_{n}^\Gamma(B,A\cap B)\cong H_{n}^\Gamma(G,A), \forall n<4$.
<!-- end thm-3 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
\label{excision proof}
	We prove the second statement, involving an interior cover of hypergraph $G=(V,E)$, $\mathbb{U}=\{A,B\}$. By $\ref{lem:Gamma-localization}$ we have $C_{n}^\Gamma(G,\mathbb{U})=C_{n}^\Gamma(G)$. Note that $C_{n}^\Gamma(G,\mathbb{U})=C_{n}^\Gamma(A)+C_{n}^\Gamma(B)$ and $C_{n}^\Gamma(A\cap B)=C_{n}\Gamma(A)\cap C_{n}^\Gamma(B)$. Furthermore, the map \[\frac{C_{n}^\Gamma(B)}{C_{n}^\Gamma(A)\cap C_{n}^\Gamma(B)}\rightarrow \frac{C_{n}^\Gamma(A)+C_{n}^\Gamma(B)}{C_{n}^\Gamma(A)}\] induced by inclusion is an isomorphism. Thus,
	\[C_{n}^\Gamma(B,A\cap B)=\frac{C_{n}^\Gamma(B)}{C_{n}^\Gamma(A\cap B)}\cong \frac{C_{n}^\Gamma(A)+C_{n}^\Gamma(B)}{C_{n}^\Gamma(A)}\cong \frac{C_{n}^\Gamma(G,\mathbb{U})}{C_{n}^\Gamma(A)}\cong \frac{C_{n}^\Gamma(G)}{C_{n}^\Gamma(A)}=C_{n}^\Gamma(G,A).\] It follows $H_{n}^\Gamma(G,A)\cong H_{n}^\Gamma(B,A\cap B)$.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- def-5: body_md -->
Let $G=(V,E)$ be the hypergraph, we define $k$-level closure and $k$-level interior for any subhypergraph $G'$, for $k\ge 0$, to be induced subhypergraph of $G$ whose vertex sets are given by, 

\begin{equation*} \begin{split}
    V(\operatorname{cl}^0(G'))=V', & ~~~~ V(\operatorname{cl}^{i}(G')) = V(\operatorname{cl}^{i-1}(\operatorname{cl}(G'))), ~~\text{for some positive integer } i,\\
V(\operatorname{int}^0(G')) =V', & ~~~~ V(\operatorname{int}^i(G'))=V(\operatorname{int}^{i-1}(\operatorname{int}(G'))), ~~ \text{for some positive integer } i.\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\medskip
<!-- end def-5 -->
<!-- lem-3: body_md -->
\label{iterative int and cl}
Let $G=(V, E)$ be the hypergraph and $G_1$ and $G_2$ be any subhypergraph of $G$. Then:
\begin{enumerate}
	\item ${\operatorname{cl}^{i}(G')} \subseteq {\operatorname{cl}^{i+1}(G')}$, $\operatorname{int}^{i}(G')\subseteq \operatorname{int}^{i-1}(\operatorname{int}(G'))$
	\item  $\operatorname{int}^i(G-G')=G-\operatorname{cl}^i(G')$, $G-\operatorname{int}^i(G')=\operatorname{cl}(G-G').$
	\item $G=\operatorname{int}^i(G_1)\cup \operatorname{int}^i(G_2)$ if and only if $\operatorname{cl}^i(G-G_2)\subseteq \operatorname{int}^i(G_1).$
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lem-3 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
The statements follow directly from the definitions by straightforward inductive arguments.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- prop-6: body_md -->
\label{gamma excion-like}

Let $G=(V,E)$ be hypergraph. Let $G_1=(V_1,E(V_1))$ and $G_2=(V_2,E(V_2))$ be subhypergraph with $\operatorname{cl}^i(G_1)\subseteq \operatorname{int}^i(G_2)$. Then the inclusion $(G-G_1,G_2-G_1)\rightarrow (G,G_2)$ induces isomorpohisms $H_{n}^\Gamma(G-G_1,G_2-G_1)\cong H_{n}^\Gamma(G,G_2)$ for all $n< 4i$. Equivalently, for interior cover $\{A,B\}$ of hypergraph $G=(V,E)$ the inclusion $(B,A\cap B)\rightarrow (G,A)$ induces isomorphisms $H_{n}^\Gamma(B,A\cap B)\cong H_{n}^\Gamma(G,A), \forall n<4i$.
<!-- end prop-6 -->
<!-- lem-4: body_md -->
\label{x-x'=2}
    Let $x,x'\in V_n^\Gamma$ with $|x-x'|=2$ then:
        $$x' \in V_{\operatorname{cl}(x)}.$$
<!-- end lem-4 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
Let $x=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)$ and $x'=(x'_1,\ldots,x'_n)$. Define, 
\[R_i:V_n^\Gamma\rightarrow V_n^\Gamma ~~\text{by}~~ (x_1\ldots,x_n)\mapsto (x_1,\ldots,x_{i-1},1-x_i,x_{i+1},\ldots,x_n) .\]
Without loss of generality we can assume that $x'=R_i R_j(x),~ \text{where}~i,j\in \{1,\ldots,n\}$ and $i\ne j$. Let $y=R_i(x)$. It follows $|x-y|=1$ and $|y-x'|=1$. Furthermore, $x,x'\in e_y$ by definition of $J_n^\Gamma.$ Since $x'\in e_y$ and $e_y\cap \{x\}\neq \phi$, $x'\in V_{\operatorname{cl}(x)}.$
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- def-6: body_md -->
Let $J_n^\Gamma$ be a $\Gamma$-hypercube and let $x \in V_n^\Gamma$.
For $m\ge 0$, define
\[
T_m(x)=\{t\in V_n^\Gamma : |t-x|\le m\}.
\]
<!-- end def-6 -->
<!-- lem-5: body_md -->
\label{closure and T_m}
Let $J_{2n}^\Gamma=(V_{2n}^\Gamma,E_{2n}^\Gamma)$ denote the $\Gamma$-hypercube
and let $x\in V_n^\Gamma$. For $k\ge0$, the hypergraph $\operatorname{cl}^k(x)$ is the induced subhypergraph
of $J_{2n}^\Gamma$ whose vertex set is $T_{2k}(x)$. Therefore, for $x\in V_n^\Gamma$, $\operatorname{cl}^n(x)=J_{2n}^\Gamma.$
<!-- end lem-5 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
We argue by induction on $k$.
 
For $k=0$, Lemma~\ref{x-x'=2} implies that the vertex set of
$\operatorname{cl}^0(x)$ consists only of $x$. Hence
\[
V_{\operatorname{cl}^0(x)}=\{x\}=T_0(x).
\]
\\
Assume now that $V_{\operatorname{cl}^k(x)}=T_{2k}(x)$.
Since $\operatorname{cl}^{k+1}(x)=\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{cl}^k(x))$, every vertex of $\operatorname{cl}^{k+1}(x)$
is either in $\operatorname{cl}^k(x)$ or is at distance $2$ from some vertex
$y\in \operatorname{cl}^k(x)$.
Let $z$ be such a vertex. Then $|y-z|=2$, and since
$y\in T_{2k}(x)$ we have $|y-x|\le 2k$.
By the triangle inequality,
\[
|z-x|\le |z-y|+|y-x|\le 2+2k=2k+2,
\]
so $z\in T_{2k+2}(x)$.
\\
Conversely, if $z\in T_{2k+2}(x)$, then $|z-x|\le 2k+2$.
If $|z-x|\le 2k$ then $z\in\operatorname{cl}^k(x)$ by the induction hypothesis.
Otherwise $|z-x|=2k+2$, and there exists a vertex $y$
with $|y-x|\le 2k$ and $|z-y|=2$.
Thus $y\in\operatorname{cl}^k(x)$ and Lemma~\ref{x-x'=2} implies that
$z\in\operatorname{cl}^{k+1}(x)$.
\\
Therefore, $V_{\operatorname{cl}^{k+1}(x)}=T_{2k+2}(x)$.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- lem-6: body_md -->
\label{cl of vertex}
Let $f: G\to G'$ be a hypergraph morphism and let $v$ be a vertex of $G$.
Then
\[
f(\operatorname{cl}(v))\subseteq \operatorname{cl}(f(v)).
\]
<!-- end lem-6 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
Let $x\in f(\operatorname{cl}(v))$. Then there exists $y\in \operatorname{cl}(v)$ such that
$f(y)=x$.\\
 
By the definition of closure, there exists a hyperedge $e$ of $G$
such that $v,y\in e$.
Since $f$ is a hypergraph morphism, there exists a hyperedge
$e'$ of $G'$ with
\[
f(e)\subseteq e'.
\]
In particular, $f(v),f(y)\in e'$.
Thus $x=f(y)$ lies in a hyperedge of $G'$ containing $f(v)$,
and therefore $x\in \operatorname{cl}(f(v))$.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- lem-7: body_md -->
\label{gamma interior}
Let $G=(V,E)$ be a hypergraph and let $A$ be a subhypergraph. Let $x\in V_n^\Gamma$ and let
$\sigma:J_n^\Gamma\to G$ be a hypergraph morphism. If
$\sigma(x)\in V(\operatorname{int}^{i}(A))$, then
\[
\sigma(N(x,J_n^\Gamma))\subseteq V(\operatorname{int}^{i-1}(A)).
\]
<!-- end lem-7 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
Let $y\in \sigma(N(x,J_n^\Gamma))$. Then there exists
$z\in N(x,J_n^\Gamma)$ such that $\sigma(z)=y$.
Since $\sigma$ is a hypergraph morphism, it follows that
$y\in N(\sigma(x),G)$.\\
 
Suppose, for contradiction, that $y\notin V(\operatorname{int}^{i-1}(A))$.
By the definition of interior,
\[
V(\operatorname{int}^{i-1}(A))=V(G)- V(\operatorname{cl}^{i-1}(G-A)),
\]
and hence $y\in V(\operatorname{cl}^{i-1}(G-A))$.
Since $y\in N(\sigma(x),G)$, this implies
$\sigma(x)\in V(\operatorname{cl}^{i}(G-A))$.
Therefore
\[
\sigma(x)\notin V(\operatorname{int}^{i}(A))
= V(G)- V(\operatorname{cl}^{i}(G-A)),
\]
which contradicts the assumption that
$\sigma(x)\in V(\operatorname{int}^{i}(A))$.\\
 
Thus $y\in V(\operatorname{int}^{i-1}(A))$, and therefore
\[
\sigma(N(x,J_n^\Gamma))\subseteq V(\operatorname{int}^{i-1}(A)).
\]
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- lem-8: body_md -->
\label{gamma excision-like proof}
	Let $G=(V, E)$ be the hypergraph, $G_1$ and $G_2$ be any two subhypergraphs such that there is some positive integer $i$ with $G=\operatorname{int}^i(G_1)\cup \operatorname{int}^i(G_2)$. Then for $n\leq 4i$ and for every $(n,\Gamma)$-hypercube $\sigma: J_n^\Gamma \rightarrow G$, $Im(\sigma)\subset G_1$ or $Im(\sigma) \subset G_2.$
<!-- end lem-8 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
Let $\sigma$ be a $(n,\Gamma)$-hypercube and $x\in V^\Gamma.$ Note that by lemma $\ref{closure and T_m}$, $T_{4i}=V_n^\Gamma$. Therefore, we show that either $\sigma(T_{4i})\subseteq G_1$ or $\sigma(T_{4i})\subseteq G_2$. Without loss of generality let  $\sigma(T_0(x))\subset \operatorname{int}^i(G_1)$. Then from \ref{closure and T_m} and \ref{gamma interior},  
\[\sigma(T_2(x))\subseteq \operatorname{int}^{i-1}(G_1)\] 
and iteratively we have $\sigma(T_{2i}(x))\subseteq \operatorname{int}^{i-i}(G_1)=G_1$.\\ 
Now if $\sigma(T_{4i}-T_{2i})\subseteq G_1$, then we have the desired result. If $\sigma(T_{4i}-T_{2i})\not\subseteq G_1$ then \[\sigma(T_{2i})\subseteq G-G_1, \sigma(T_{2i+2})\subseteq \operatorname{cl}(G-G_1).\] Iteration over $i$ gives $\sigma(T_{2i+2i})\subseteq \operatorname{cl}^i(G-G_1).$ Now by lemma \ref{iterative int and cl}, 
\[\operatorname{cl}^i(G-G_1)\subseteq\operatorname{int}^i(G_2).\] Thus, $\sigma(T_{4i})\subseteq \operatorname{int}^i(G_2)$ and the result follows.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
Proof follows in the same pattern as the proof of \ref{gamma excision} by using [\ref{gamma excision-like proof}]
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- lem-9: body_md -->
\label{box excision lemma}
Let $G=(V,E)$ be the hypergraph, $G_1$ and $G_2$ be any two subhypergraph with  $G=\operatorname{int}(G_1)\cup \operatorname{int}(G_2)$. Then for $n\leq 1$ and for every $(n,\Box)$-hyppercube $\sigma$, $Im(\sigma)\subset G_1$ or $Im(\sigma) \subset G_2.$ In particular, $C_n^\Box(G)=C_n^\Box(G,\mathbb{U})$, where $\mathbb{U}=\{G_1,G_2\}$ and $n\in\{0,1\}$.
<!-- end lem-9 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
Note that by definition, $C_n^\Box(G,\mathbb{U}) \subset C_n^\Box(G)$. For converse we proceed through induction on $n$\\


For $n=0$, let $\sigma \in  C_0^\Box(G)$. Clearly, either $Im(\sigma) \in \operatorname{int}(G_1)$ or $Im(\sigma) \in \operatorname{int}(G_2)$. It implies $C_0^\Box(G)\subseteq C_0^\Box(G,\mathbb{U})$.\\


For $n=1$, in this case, the set $Im(\sigma) \subset X$ comprises two elements, namely, $\sigma(0)$ and $\sigma(1)$. We can assume without loss of generality that the element $\sigma(0) \in \operatorname{int}(G_1)$. Then by definition of hypergraph morphism $\sigma(0)\in e$, for some hyperedge $e$ in $G_1.$ Note that, $\sigma(1)\in e$, since $\{0,1\}$ is a hyperedge in $J_1^\Box$ we get $Im(\sigma) \subset G_1$.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- ex-9: body_md -->
Let $G$ be the hypergraph with vertex set $V=\{v_1,v_2,v_3,v_4\}$ and set of hyperedges $E=\{\{v_1,v_2\} , \{v_2,v_3\}, \{v_3,v_4\}\}$. Let vertex set of $G_1$ and $G_2$ be $\{v_1,v_2,v_3\} $ and $ \{v_2,v_3,v_4\} $, respectively. Then note that $\operatorname{int}(G_1)=\{v_1,v_2\}$ and $\operatorname{int}(G_2)=\{v_3,v_4\}$ Define $\sigma: J_2^\Box \rightarrow G$ by $\sigma(0,0)=v_1$, $\sigma(1,0)=v_2$,  $\sigma(0,1)=v_3$ and $\sigma(1,1)=v_4$. Note that $Im(\sigma)\notin G_i$ for $i=\{1,2\}.$
<!-- end ex-9 -->
<!-- lem-10: body_md -->
\label{lemma box excision-like}
Let $G=(V,E)$ be the hypergraph, $G_1$ and $G_2$ be any two subhypergraphs such that there is some positive integer $i$ with  $G=\operatorname{int}^i(G_1)\cup \operatorname{int}^i(G_2)$. Then for $n\leq i+1$ and for every $(n,\Box)$-hyppercube $\sigma$, $Im(\sigma)\subset G_1$ or $Im(\sigma) \subset G_2.$ In particular, $C_n^\Box(G)=C_n^\Box(G,\mathbb{U})$, where $\mathbb{U}=\{G_1,G_2\}$ and $n\leq i+1.$
<!-- end lem-10 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
Let $\sigma$ be a $(n,\Box)$-hypercube and fix $x=(0,0,\ldots,0) \in V_n^\Box$. For $n=0$,  $\sigma(T_0(x)) \subset   \operatorname{int}(G_1)$.  
Then, by the definition of hypergraph morphism,
\[
 {Im}(\sigma) \subset   \operatorname{int}(G_1).
\]
For $0 \le n \le i+1$, without loss of generality let
\[ \sigma(T_0(x)) \subset   \operatorname{int}^i(G_1). \]
Since elements of $T_{j-1}(x)$ and $T_{j+1}(x)$ are neighbors of $T_j(x)$ for $j=1,2,\ldots, n-1 $, we have
\[
\sigma(T_j(x)) \subset   \operatorname{int}^{i-j}(G_1), \text{ by definition of $k$-level interior}.\]
Now, for $n=i+1,$ $\sigma(T_n(x)-T_{n-1}(x))$ may or may not be in the vertex set of $G_1$; if it is, we have the desired result, and if it is not, then we have $\sigma(T_n(x)-T_{n-1}(x))\subset G-G_1$, and we claim that $Im(\sigma)\subset G_2$. Since we know that from \ref{iterative int and cl}, \[G-G_1\subset \operatorname{cl}(G-G_1)\subset \operatorname{cl}^i(G-G_1)\subseteq \operatorname{int}^i(G_2).\] It implies $\sigma(T_n(x)-T_{n-1}(x))\subset \operatorname{int}^i(G_2)$ and using the definition of $k$-level interior and for  $j=2,\ldots,n$ we have $\sigma(T_{n}(x)-T_{n-j-1}(x))\subseteq \operatorname{int}^{i-j+1}(G_2)$. Thus, $Im(\sigma)\subset G_2$.
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- thm-4: body_md -->
(Excision-like property)\\
Let $G=(V,E)$ be hypergraph. Let $G_1=(V_1,E(V_1))$ and $G_2=(V_2,E(V_2))$ be subhypergraph such that $G_1\subseteq G_2$ and $cl^i(G_1)\subseteq  \operatorname{int}^i(G_2)$. Then the inclusion $(G-G_1,G_2-G_1)\rightarrow (G,G_2)$ induces isomorpohisms $H_{n}^\Box(G-G_1,G_2-G_1)\cong H_{n}^\Box(G,G_2)$ for all $n< i+1$. Equivalently, for interior cover $\{A,B\}$ of hypergraph $G=(V,E)$ the inclusion $(B,A\cap B)\rightarrow (G,A)$ induces isomorphisms $H_{n}^\Box(B,A\cap B)\cong H_{n}^\Box(G,A), \forall n<i+1$.
<!-- end thm-4 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
The proof follows from Lemma \ref{lemma box excision-like}
<!-- end proof-20 -->
